claim: Mice show a rapid, profound reduction in voluntary running wheel activity (RWA) as soon as pregnancy is achieved.
source: As part of the maternal adaptations to pregnancy, mice show a rapid, profound reduction in voluntary running wheel activity (RWA) as soon as pregnancy is achieved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing RWA measurements in pregnant mice.

claim: Prolactin can acutely suppress RWA in non-pregnant female mice.
source: We show that prolactin can acutely suppress RWA in non-pregnant female mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from prolactin treatment studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Conditional deletion of prolactin receptors (Prlr) from most forebrain neurons prevented the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
source: conditional deletion of prolactin receptors (Prlr) from either most forebrain neurons or from GABA neurons prevented the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: Conditional deletion of prolactin receptors (Prlr) from GABA neurons prevented the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
source: conditional deletion of prolactin receptors (Prlr) from either most forebrain neurons or from GABA neurons prevented the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of Prlr specifically from the medial preoptic area completely abolished the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
source: Deletion of Prlr specifically from the medial preoptic area, a brain region associated with multiple homeostatic and behavioral roles including parental behavior, completely abolished the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-cre injection studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: As pregnancy progresses, prolactin action continues to contribute to the further suppression of RWA, although it is not the only factor involved.
source: As pregnancy progresses, prolactin action continues to contribute to the further suppression of RWA, although it is not the only factor involved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RWA differences between knockout and control mice in late pregnancy.

claim: The sustained changes in metabolic rate typical of pregnancy have been described as 'at the limits of human physical capability,' similar to that expended in extreme physical activity such as an ultramarathon, but over a longer timeframe.
source: The sustained changes in metabolic rate typical of pregnancy have been described as 'at the limits of human physical capability,' similar to that expended in extreme physical activity such as an ultramarathon, but over a longer timeframe (Thurber et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thurber et al., 2019.

claim: Hormonal changes associated with pregnancy drive a wide range of adaptations to maternal physiology, and in particular, complex changes in metabolic function.
source: To enable the pregnant female to cope with these demands, hormonal changes associated with pregnancy drive a wide range of adaptations to maternal physiology, and in particular, complex changes in metabolic function (Napso et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Napso et al., 2018.

claim: Pregnant female mice rapidly lower their energy expenditure and physical activity levels, as measured by daily voluntary running wheel activity.
source: Using a mouse model to characterize metabolic adaptations in pregnancy, we have shown that along with increases in energy intake, pregnant females rapidly lower their energy expenditure and physical activity levels, as measured by daily voluntary running wheel activity (RWA; Ladyman et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ladyman et al., 2018a and experimental data in the current manuscript.

claim: The reduction in RWA starts very early in pregnancy before there is any significant increase in metabolic load, even before implantation.
source: Remarkably, however, the reduction in RWA starts very early in pregnancy before there is any significant increase in metabolic load, even before implantation (Ladyman et al., 2018a; Slonaker, 1925)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ladyman et al., 2018a and Slonaker, 1925, and experimental data in the current manuscript.

claim: The reduction in RWA can be considered an anticipatory adaptation in preparation for the future metabolic demands.
source: and thus, can be considered an anticipatory adaptation in preparation for the future metabolic demands
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that RWA reduction occurs before metabolic load increases.

claim: One of the very first changes in hormones in pregnancy is the mating-induced initiation of twice-daily prolactin surges that are required to maintain corpus luteum function in the ovary to sustain the pregnancy.
source: In rodents, one of the very first changes in hormones in pregnancy is the mating-induced initiation of twice-daily prolactin surges that are required to maintain corpus luteum function in the ovary to sustain the pregnancy (Phillipps et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Phillipps et al., 2020.

claim: Figure 1A depicts daily RWA from a single representative female mouse during different reproductive states, showing the cyclical running patterns characteristic of the estrous cycle with increased running preceding each ovulation.
source: Figure 1A depicts daily RWA from a single representative female mouse during different reproductive states, showing the cyclical running patterns characteristic of the estrous cycle with increased running preceding each ovulation
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Figure 1A shows profound reductions in RWA during pregnancy and lactation, apart from a brief increase in RWA the night after birth.
source: profound reductions in RWA during pregnancy and lactation, apart from a brief increase in RWA the night after birth
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Figure 1A shows the rapid return to non-pregnant levels of RWA following weaning of pups.
source: and the rapid return to non-pregnant levels of RWA following weaning of pups
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The saucer wheel has less resistance and the possibility of 'coasting' on the wheel may lead to higher RWA being detected compared to the upright wheel.
source: whereas the saucer wheel has less resistance and the possibility of 'coasting' on the wheel may lead to higher RWA being detected (as suggested by the higher average 'distance' measured in the saucer group vs. the upright wheel group, Figure 1B, p<0.0001, t = 4.608, df = 60) (De Bono et al., 2006; Girard et al., 2001; Manzanares et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and citations to De Bono et al., 2006; Girard et al., 2001; Manzanares et al., 2018.

claim: All mice showed a rapid reduction in RWA early in pregnancy regardless of the different equipment used.
source: Regardless of the different equipment, all mice showed a rapid reduction in RWA early in pregnancy (Figure 1C, significant effect of time p<0.0001, F(21, 1163) = 1163 and Figure 1D, significant effect of physiological state [non-pregnant, non-lactating control, henceforth referred to as 'non-pregnant' group] vs. early pregnancy: p<0.0001, F(1, 47) = 133.8, Sidak's multiple comparisons; non-pregnant vs. early pregnancy: upright wheel p<0.0001, t = 7.887, df = 47; saucer wheel p<0.0001, t = 8.461, df = 47)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: The rapid reduction in RWA early in pregnancy is a robust behavioral change induced as early as the first day of pregnancy.
source: demonstrating that this is a robust behavioral change induced as early as the first day of pregnancy
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RWA changes on the first day of pregnancy.

claim: During the dark phase following the first observation of pups, RWA was significantly increased compared to either the dark phase immediately before the day of birth or the second dark phase after pups were born/observed.
source: During the dark phase following the first observation of pups, RWA was significantly increased compared to either the dark phase immediately before the day of birth or the second dark phase after pups were born/observed (significant effect of time p<0.0001, F(2, 110) = 43.10, Sidak's multiple comparisons: day before birth vs. day of birth p<0.0001, t = 8.671, DF = 110.0; day of birth vs. day after birth p<0.0001, t = 7.210, DF = 110.0; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in RWA on the day of birth was observed in 88% of mice (50 out of 57).
source: This increase was observed in 88% of mice (50 out of 57)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data counting the number of mice showing the effect.

claim: The increase in RWA on the day of birth is likely to be associated with the hormonal changes that drive the postpartum ovulation in mice.
source: and is likely to be associated with the hormonal changes that drive the postpartum ovulation in mice, although this was not further investigated
evidence: This claim is speculative as the authors state it was not further investigated.

claim: Pregnancy significantly influenced both energy expenditure and total daily ambulation in female C57BL/6J mice without access to running wheels.
source: We observed that pregnancy significantly influenced both energy expenditure (Figure 1E, repeated measures ANOVA p=0.0002, F(1.457, 7.286) = 39.86) and total daily ambulation (Figure 1F, repeated measures ANOVA p=0.005, F(2.063, 8.253) = 10.24).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Both energy expenditure and ambulation were significantly reduced in early pregnancy compared to the non-pregnant state.
source: Both energy expenditure (Figure 1F, paired t-test p=0.03, t = 2.812, df = 5) and ambulation (Figure 1G paired t-test p=0.03, t = 3.121, df = 4) were significantly reduced in early pregnancy compared to the non-pregnant state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: Early pregnancy is associated with reduced physical activity, independent of the actual form of physical activity measured.
source: This suggests that early pregnancy is associated with reduced physical activity, independent of the actual form of physical activity measured.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that both RWA and ambulation are reduced in early pregnancy.

claim: When mice are housed with running wheels, the reduction in physical activity is only detected as a major reduction in RWA, likely because this accounts for by far the greatest proportion of their overall physical activity levels.
source: When mice are housed with running wheels, this reduction in physical activity is only detected as a major reduction in RWA, likely because this accounts for by far the greatest proportion of their overall physical activity levels (Ladyman et al., 2018a)
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Ladyman et al., 2018a.

claim: When housed without running wheels, the reduction in physical activity is detected in home cage ambulation, which is the predominant form of physical activity in this situation.
source: whereas in the current study, when housed without running wheels, the reduction in physical activity is detected in home cage ambulation, which is the predominant form of physical activity in this situation
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The reduction in RWA persisted throughout pregnancy and lactation, conditions characterized by high prolactin.
source: This idea was supported by the observation that the reduction in RWA persisted throughout pregnancy and lactation (Figure 1A), conditions characterized by high prolactin (Phillipps et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and a citation to Phillipps et al., 2020.

claim: Prolactin treatment led to a significant reduction in RWA in female mice, particularly in the first 3 hr of the dark phase.
source: Prolactin treatment led to a significant reduction in RWA (Figure 2A, repeated measures two-way ANOVA, interaction time × treatment p<0.0001, F(13, 286) = 6.684, and Figure 2B, paired t-test p = 0.007, t = 3.28, df = 11), particularly in the first 3 hr of the dark phase (Figure 2A, Sidak's multiple comparisons test: vehicle vs. prolactin 1 hr p=0.0009 [t = 5.107, df = 18.65], 2 hr p = 0.0173 [t = 3.736, df = 20.61], 3 hr p=0.0248 [t = 3.742, df = 15.91])
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: No effect of acute prolactin treatment on RWA activity was observed in male mice.
source: No effect of acute prolactin treatment on RWA activity was observed in male mice (repeated measures two-way ANOVA, interaction time × treatment p=0.9222, F(13, 286) = 0.5028, and paired Student's t-test p=0.8732, t = 0.1634, df = 11; Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: C57BL/6J female mice ran significantly more per 24 hr than male mice.
source: In accordance with previously published work (reviewed in Manzanares et al., 2018), our C57BL/6J female mice ran significantly more per 24 hr than male mice (comparison between vehicle-treated females and males from Figure 2B and D, Student's t-test p<0.0001, t = 8.547, df = 22).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Manzanares et al., 2018.

claim: Prolactin injection an hour prior to testing did not influence distance traveled by female mice in a novel environment.
source: In a novel environment, such as in an open field or the elevated plus maze (EPM) paradigm, prolactin injection an hour prior to testing did not influence distance traveled by female mice (Figure 3A and B), suggesting that there is not a generalized effect on locomotion (Student's t-test, EPM: p = 0.119, t = 1.661, df = 14, open field test [OFT]: p=0.1177, t = 1.667, df = 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: There is not a generalized effect of prolactin on locomotion.
source: suggesting that there is not a generalized effect on locomotion
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that prolactin did not affect distance traveled in novel environments.

claim: Prolactin treatment led to a significant reduction in ambulation during the 12 hr of the dark phase of the light cycle in the home cage environment.
source: Prolactin treatment led to a significant reduction in ambulation during the 12 hr of the dark phase of the light cycle (Figure 3C, repeated measures ANOVA, interaction time × treatment, p=0.016, F(13, 234) = 2.079), although this was a subtle effect and only evident in the late stages of the dark phase (Figure 3C, Sidak's multiple comparisons test: vehicle vs. prolactin 12 hr p=0.03, t = 3.7, df = 12.6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: Prolactin treatment tended to increase, rather than decrease, total beam breaks, although there was no significant difference detected.
source: Interestingly, when total counts of XY beam breaks were examined, prolactin treatment tended to increase, rather than decrease, total beam breaks, although there was no significant difference detected (Figure 3D, repeated measures ANOVA, interaction time × treatment p=0.078, F(13, 234) = 1.628).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: Prolactin treatment significantly increased fine movement beam breaks, defined as beam breaks that are not in a consecutive direction, thus indicating non-ambulatory (stationary) movement.
source: Further examination indicated that prolactin treatment significantly increased fine movement beam breaks, defined as beam breaks that are not in a consecutive direction, thus indicating non-ambulatory (stationary) movement (Figure 3E, repeated measures ANOVA, interaction time × treatment, p<0.0001, F(13, 117) = 183.9, post hoc analysis: vehicle vs. prolactin, p<0.05 for hours 5–12, t ranges from t = 3.038–4.119, df = 117).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference identified in the time spent doing any of these behaviors following prolactin or vehicle injection except for time spent 'still, off nest,' which was slightly yet significantly reduced in the prolactin-treated group.
source: There was no difference identified in the time spent doing any of these behaviors following prolactin or vehicle injection except for time spent 'still, off nest,' which was slightly yet significantly reduced in the prolactin-treated group (Figure 3G, paired Student's t-tests, 'still, off nest': p = 0.047, t = 2.261, df = 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: Prolactin reduces voluntary RWA in female mice, but had little or no significant impact on general ambulation levels in either a novel environment or in the home cage.
source: Overall, this set of experiments demonstrated that prolactin reduces voluntary RWA in female mice, but had little or no significant impact on general ambulation levels in either a novel environment or in the home cage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing differential effects of prolactin on RWA versus ambulation.

claim: While rapid changes in RWA activity in early pregnancy may be driven by mating-induced prolactin surges, there is no evidence to support a similar mechanism underlying reductions in ambulation in early pregnancy.
source: Therefore, while rapid changes in RWA activity in early pregnancy may be driven by mating-induced prolactin surges, there is no evidence to support a similar mechanism underlying reductions in ambulation in early pregnancy (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of prolactin on RWA versus ambulation.

claim: Prlr are highly expressed in the hypothalamus, mostly localized to the arcuate, ventromedial (VMN), paraventricular (PVN), anteroventral periventricular nuclei, and the preoptic area (POA).
source: In mice, Prlr are highly expressed in the hypothalamus, mostly localized to the arcuate, ventromedial (VMN), paraventricular (PVN), anteroventral periventricular nuclei, and the preoptic area (POA) (Brown et al., 2010; Kokay et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2010 and Kokay et al., 2018.

claim: Within the POA, there is high expression of Prlr in the median, periventricular, and medial regions.
source: Within the POA, there is high expression of Prlr in the median, periventricular, and medial regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Prlr expression patterns.

claim: Lower expression of Prlr is observed in the anterior hypothalamic area and dorsomedial hypothalamus.
source: Lower expression is observed in the anterior hypothalamic area and dorsomedial hypothalamus.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Prlr expression patterns.

claim: Outside of the hypothalamus, the medial amygdala, anterior bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), lateral septum, and periaqueductal gray also have robust Prlr expression.
source: Outside of the hypothalamus, the medial amygdala, anterior bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), lateral septum, and periaqueductal gray also have robust Prlr expression (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2010.

claim: Expression of Prlr in the hypothalamus does not appear to undergo significant modification during pregnancy and lactation, except for an increase in the arcuate nucleus detected in late pregnancy in the rat.
source: Expression of Prlr in the hypothalamus does not appear to undergo significant modification during pregnancy and lactation, except for an increase in the arcuate nucleus detected in late pregnancy in the rat (Augustine et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Augustine et al., 2003.

claim: During pregnancy, elevated levels of phosphorylation of the transcription factor signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (pSTAT5) are detected throughout the brain.
source: During pregnancy, elevated levels of phosphorylation of the transcription factor signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (pSTAT5) are detected throughout the brain.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about pSTAT5 expression during pregnancy.

claim: pSTAT5 is a well-characterized intracellular signaling molecule-activated downstream of the Prlr (and a range of other cytokines).
source: This is a well-characterized intracellular signaling molecule-activated downstream of the Prlr (and a range of other cytokines)
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about pSTAT5 signaling.

claim: The majority of pSTAT5 in the brain during pregnancy is caused by increased Prlr activation.
source: but we have shown that the majority of pSTAT5 in the brain during pregnancy is caused by increased Prlr activation (Gustafson et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2020.

claim: Increased pSTAT5 in the brain during pregnancy is caused both by surges in prolactin early in pregnancy and by rising placental lactogen as pregnancy progresses.
source: both by surges in prolactin early in pregnancy and by rising placental lactogen as pregnancy progresses (Phillipps et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Phillipps et al., 2020.

claim: During lactation, various regions within the brain show increased prolactin-induced pSTAT5 expression compared to mice in the diestrous phase of the estrous cycle, including the medial POA, BNST, PVN, and medial amygdala.
source: During lactation, various regions within the brain show increased prolactin-induced pSTAT5 expression compared to mice in the diestrous phase of the estrous cycle, including the medial POA, BNST, PVN, and medial amygdala (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: In the Prlrlox/lox mouse line, in the presence of Cre-recombinase the sequence between the loxP sites of the Prlr gene undergoes inversion, resulting in the deletion of exons 5–10 of the Prlr gene and induced expression of enhanced green fluorescent protein (GFP).
source: Our Prlrlox/lox mouse line is constructed such that in the presence of Cre-recombinase the sequence between the loxP sites of the Prlr gene undergoes inversion, resulting in the deletion of exons 5–10 of the Prlr gene and induced expression of enhanced green fluorescent protein (GFP) (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2016 describing the mouse line construction.

claim: In the Prlrlox/lox mouse line, GFP is a useful marker of cells in which Cre-mediated recombination (and therefore Prlr deletion) has taken place.
source: Thus, in this mouse line, GFP is a useful marker of cells in which Cre-mediated recombination (and therefore Prlr deletion) has taken place.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic construction of the mouse line.

claim: In the MPOA, there was a significant reduction of Prlr from GABAergic neurons in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.
source: In the MPOA, there was a significant reduction of Prlr from GABAergic neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test, p=0.0091, U = 0).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlr is not significantly reduced in the PVN in the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.
source: As previously shown, Prlr is not significantly reduced in the PVN in the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test PVN: p=0.6065, U = 26; Gustafson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Gustafson et al., 2020.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice do not show normal 4- to 5-day estrous cycles due to hyperprolactinemia caused by a lack of negative feedback in the hypothalamus.
source: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice do not show normal 4- to 5-day estrous cycles (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, Mann–Whitney test, p<0.0001, U = 0) due to hyperprolactinemia caused by a lack of negative feedback in the hypothalamus (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, and a citation to Brown et al., 2016.

claim: The high prolactin in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice acts in the ovary to prolong progesterone secretion after each ovulation, resulting in serial pseudopregnancy-like phases of around 10–12 days between ovulations.
source: The high prolactin acts in the ovary to prolong progesterone secretion after each ovulation, resulting in serial pseudopregnancy-like phases of around 10–12 days between ovulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed estrous cycle patterns and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There was a trend for reduced RWA in non-pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre compared to control mice in the same state.
source: We observed a trend for reduced RWA in non-pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre compared to control mice (Prlrlox/lox) in the same state (Figure 4B, t-test, p=0.058, t = 1.984, df = 27)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: Non-pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showed an absence of the cyclical pattern of elevated RWA prior to ovulation that has previously been described.
source: and in particular, the absence of the cyclical pattern of elevated RWA prior to ovulation that has previously been described (Ladyman et al., 2018a; Basterfield et al., 2009; Lightfoot, 2008; Rosenfeld, 2017; Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Ladyman et al., 2018a; Basterfield et al., 2009; Lightfoot, 2008; Rosenfeld, 2017.

claim: The cumulative RWA activity over 5 days showed no difference between Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and control genotypes.
source: The cumulative RWA activity over 5 days (to take into account the 4- to 5-day estrous cycle observed in our control mice) showed no difference between genotypes (Figure 4D, p=0.0831, t = 1.802, df = 26)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D with statistical analysis.

claim: The absence of estrous cycle-induced changes in the RWA of Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre did not significantly impact on total amount of RWA.
source: suggesting that the absence of estrous cycle-induced changes in the RWA of Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre did not significantly impact on total amount of RWA
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that cumulative RWA was similar between genotypes.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice had slightly increased body weight in the non-pregnant state compared to controls.
source: Despite the abnormal cycles and slightly increased body weight (Student's t-test, p=0.0156, t = 2.570, df = 29) in the non-pregnant state (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice are able to become pregnant and maintain a pregnancy, showing no differences in fetus number and uterus mass in late pregnancy or litter size on day 4 of lactation compared to controls.
source: these mice are able to become pregnant and maintain a pregnancy, showing no differences in fetus number (Mann–Whitney test, p=0.1911, U = 16.5) and uterus mass in late pregnancy (Student's t-test p=0.4416, t = 0.7938, df = 13) or litter size on day 4 of lactation (Mann–Whitney test, p=0.1568, U = 83.5; Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–E with statistical analysis.

claim: Mice lacking Prlr in most forebrain neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) failed to show the characteristic decrease in RWA in early pregnancy, and in fact showed significantly increased RWA compared to control mice throughout pregnancy.
source: Mice lacking Prlr in most forebrain neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) failed to show the characteristic decrease in RWA in early pregnancy, and in fact showed significantly increased RWA compared to control mice throughout pregnancy (Figure 4E, interaction genotype × time, p<0.0001, F(21, 481) = 3.297).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice did not show a significant reduction in RWA in early pregnancy, whereas control mice reduced RWA to approximately 50% of non-pregnant levels in the first few days of pregnancy.
source: When analyzing the overall change in RWA across the first week of pregnancy, Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice did not show a significant reduction in RWA, whereas control mice reduced RWA to approximately 50% of non-pregnant levels in the first few days of pregnancy (Figure 4F, interaction genotype × time, p=0.0385, F(1,41) = 4.57, Sidak's multiple comparisons test between non-pregnant and early pregnant: Prlrlox/lox p=0.002 [t = 4.310, df = 41], Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre p=0.3899 [t = 1.249, df = 41]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F with statistical analysis.

claim: All pregnant mice showed a reduction in RWA over the course of pregnancy, but even when heavily pregnant on days 15–18 of pregnancy, the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre animals continued to run significantly more on the wheel than controls.
source: All pregnant mice showed a reduction in RWA over the course of pregnancy, but even when heavily pregnant on days 15–18 of pregnancy, the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre animals continued to run significantly more on the wheel than controls (Figure 4G and H, day 15 hourly RWA pattern: interaction time × genotype, p<0.0001, F(23, 621) = 4.363; total RWA on day 15, Student's t-test p=0.0035, t = 3.215, df = 26, n = 12–15 per genotype [data not shown]; days 16–18 cumulative RWA: Student's t-test p<0.0001, t = 5.037, df = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4G and 4H with statistical analysis.

claim: While weight gain and physical constraints are likely to play a major role in the overall suppression of RWA in mid-late pregnancy, prolactin action in the brain still plays a contributing role even at this stage of pregnancy.
source: These data suggest that while weight gain and physical constraints are likely to play a major role in the overall suppression of RWA in mid-late pregnancy, prolactin action in the brain still plays a contributing role even at this stage of pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that knockout mice still show higher RWA in late pregnancy.

claim: Analyzing late pregnancy (day 17) RWA with body weight as a covariate demonstrated a significant difference, independent of body weight.
source: Analyzing late pregnancy (day 17) RWA with body weight as a covariate demonstrated a significant difference, independent of body weight (ANCOVA p=0.0006, F(1,24) = 15.58).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using ANCOVA.

claim: The slightly lower gestational weight gain and slightly elevated pre-pregnancy body weight in the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre meant that by late pregnancy body mass was not significantly different between Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and controls.
source: The slightly lower gestational weight gain (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F, interaction genotype × time, p<0.0001, F(17,325) = 3.348) and slightly elevated pre-pregnancy body weight in the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) meant that by late pregnancy body mass was not significantly different between Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G, Student's t-test p=0.7885, t = 0.2711, df = 25)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, F, and G with statistical analysis.

claim: Differences in RWA in late pregnancy between genotypes cannot be attributed to body weight.
source: meaning that differences in RWA in late pregnancy between genotypes cannot be attributed to body weight
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that body weight was similar between genotypes in late pregnancy.

claim: In the presence of a running wheel, Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice gained slightly, yet significantly, less weight by the later stages of pregnancy compared to controls.
source: In the presence of a running wheel, Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice gained slightly, yet significantly, less weight by the later stages of pregnancy (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F) compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Both Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and control mice showed a pregnancy-induced increase in food intake, but there was no difference in food intake in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre compared to control mice.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3H with statistical analysis.

claim: Time spent in the open arms of the EPM was similar in both Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and control groups, suggesting no difference in anxiety-like behavior in the pregnant mice.
source: Time spent in the open arms of the EPM was similar in both groups, suggesting no difference in anxiety-like behavior in the pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3I, Student's t-test p=0.7756, t = 0.291, df = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3I with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice have more limited, although still extensive, deletion of prolactin receptors throughout the brain compared to Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.
source: These mice have more limited, although still extensive, deletion of prolactin receptors throughout the brain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test MPOA: p=0.0464, U = 15, Arc: p = 0.0014, U = 6; Brown et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations to Brown et al., 2016 and Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Approximately half the prolactin-responsive neurons in the MPOA are GABAergic.
source: In the MPOA, we have previously shown that approximately half the prolactin-responsive neurons are GABAergic (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice had a significant reduction in the number of GABA neurons that co-localize with Prlr (around 70%).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The deletion of Prlr from GABAergic neurons in Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice was not a complete deletion of Prlr from all GABAergic neurons.
source: however, it should be noted that this was not a complete deletion of Prlr from all GABAergic neurons
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing incomplete deletion.

claim: Prlr are not deleted from the majority of hypothalamic dopamine neurons in Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice, meaning that prolactin levels are normal and they have normal 4- to 5-day estrous cycles.
source: Importantly, however, Prlr are not deleted from the majority of hypothalamic dopamine neurons in this line, meaning that prolactin levels are normal and they have normal 4- to 5-day estrous cycles (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2016.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice have similar body weight in the virgin state as controls.
source: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice have similar body weight in the virgin state as controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3J, Student's t-test p=0.3962, t = 0.8718, df = 16)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3J with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice can carry a pregnancy to term, and both genotypes had similar sized litters.
source: can carry a pregnancy to term, and both genotypes had similar sized litters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K, Mann–Whitney p = 0.7734, U = 41)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K with statistical analysis.

claim: Non-pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre and control mice had similar levels of RWA.
source: Non-pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre and control (Prlrlox/lox) mice had similar levels of RWA (Figure 4I, Student's t-test p=0.5358, t = 0.6329, df = 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice had markedly higher RWA throughout pregnancy compared to controls.
source: In contrast, however, Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice had markedly higher RWA throughout pregnancy compared to controls (Figure 4F, interaction time × genotype, p=0.010, F(21, 291) = 1914).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice did not show the rapid reduction in RWA in early pregnancy, whereas control mice showed the characteristic pregnancy-induced immediate reduction in RWA.
source: Consistent with observations in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice, Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice did not show the rapid reduction in RWA in early pregnancy, whereas control mice showed the characteristic pregnancy-induced immediate reduction in RWA (Figure 4G, interaction genotype × time, p=0.0162, F(1, 23) = 6.735, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for significant effect of time: Prlrlox/lox, p=0.0007, t = 4.196, df = 23, Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre: p = 0.7888, t = 0.6215, df = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in anxiety-like behavior were detected in pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice compared to controls.
source: Again, similar to Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre, no differences in anxiety-like behavior were detected in pregnant Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3L, Student's t-test p=0.8617, t = 0.1762, df = 22).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3L with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference in body weight gain or food intake during pregnancy in Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice compared to controls.
source: While food intake and body weight increased across pregnancy (Figure 4—figure supplement 3M: body weight, effect of time, p<0.0001, F(1.413, 11.89) = 302.9; Figure 4—figure supplement 3N: food intake, effect of time, p<0.0001, F(5.283, 60.6) = 10.09), there was no difference in body weight gain or food intake during pregnancy in Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, body weight gain: effect of genotype, p = 0.4648, F(1, 15) = 0.5627; food intake: effect of genotype, p=0.3772, F(1,17) = 0.8224).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3M and 3N with statistical analysis.

claim: The attenuated reduction in RWA in early pregnancy in both Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre strongly indicates a role for prolactin action in the brain, driving early changes in RWA as soon as pregnancy is initiated.
source: Overall, the attenuated reduction in RWA in early pregnancy in both Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre strongly indicates a role for prolactin action in the brain, driving early changes in RWA as soon as pregnancy is initiated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results in both knockout mouse lines.

claim: On day 15 of pregnancy, Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice engaged in more RWA than controls.
source: On day 15 of pregnancy, Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice engaged in more RWA than controls (Figure 4L, day 15 hourly RWA pattern, interaction time × genotype, p=0.0007, F(23, 391) = 2.291; total RWA on day 15, Student's t-test p=0.0494, t = 2.116, df = 17, n = 9–10; data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L with statistical analysis.

claim: As pregnancy advanced further, RWA became similar between Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls, as shown by no significant difference in cumulative RWA over days 16–18 of pregnancy.
source: Unlike the continued higher RWA seen in the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice, as pregnancy advanced further, RWA became similar between Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls, as shown by no significant difference in cumulative RWA over days 16–18 of pregnancy (days 16–18 cumulative RWA: Mann–Whitney non-parametric test p=0.1728, U = 24).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Body weight in late pregnancy was not different between Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls.
source: Body weight in late pregnancy was not different between Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls ( Figure 4—figure supplement 3O, day 17 pregnant body weight Student's t-test p=0.1742, t = 1.437, df = 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3O with statistical analysis.

claim: In late pregnancy prolactin-induced suppression of RWA is not mediated by GABAergic neurons.
source: These results suggest that in late pregnancy prolactin-induced suppression of RWA is not mediated by GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that RWA became similar between Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre and controls in late pregnancy.

claim: Arcuate nucleus kisspeptin neurons express Prlr.
source: We have shown that arcuate kisspeptin neurons express Prlr (Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014; Kokay et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014 and Kokay et al., 2011.

claim: Prolactin is likely to inhibit the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
source: and that prolactin is likely to inhibit their activity (Brown et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: Only a small proportion of arcuate kisspeptin cells are GABAergic.
source: although it should be noted that only a small proportion of these kisspeptin cells are GABAergic (Marshall et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marshall et al., 2017.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice have normal estrous cycles.
source: We have previously shown that these mice have normal estrous cycles and have Prlr deleted specifically in the arcuate nucleus kisspeptin neurons as demonstrated by in situ hybridization for Prlr and Kiss1 mRNAs and also by the presence of enhanced GFP using immunohistochemistry (Figure 5A, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test p=0.0004, U = 0; Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice have Prlr deleted specifically in the arcuate nucleus kisspeptin neurons.
source: We have previously shown that these mice have normal estrous cycles and have Prlr deleted specifically in the arcuate nucleus kisspeptin neurons as demonstrated by in situ hybridization for Prlr and Kiss1 mRNAs and also by the presence of enhanced GFP using immunohistochemistry (Figure 5A, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test p=0.0004, U = 0; Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: In the non-pregnant state, Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre and control Prlrlox/lox mice did not differ in their mean daily RWA.
source: In the non-pregnant state, Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Creand control Prlrlox/lox mice did not differ in their mean daily RWA (Figure 5B, p=0.6604, t = 0.4472, df = 17).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant effect of pregnancy on RWA activity in both Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre and control Prlrlox/lox mice but no difference between the genotypes.
source: Overall, there was a significant effect of pregnancy on RWA activity in both Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Creand control Prlrlox/lox mice (Figure 5C, effect of time, p<0.0001, F(4.649, 60.88) = 39.98) but no difference between the genotypes (effect of genotype, p=0.8805, F(1, 14) = 0.02345).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C with statistical analysis.

claim: Both Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre and control genotypes showed the normal pregnancy-induced suppression in RWA in early pregnancy, and there was no major effect of deletion of Prlr in arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
source: In other words, both genotypes showed the normal pregnancy-induced suppression in RWA in early pregnancy, and there was no major effect of deletion of Prlr in arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that there was no difference between genotypes in pregnancy-induced RWA suppression.

claim: The effect of pregnancy on RWA in the first few days of pregnancy (days 1–3) was subtly reduced in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice compared with control mice.
source: On closer analysis of the early pregnancy change in RWA, while both genotypes showed a decrease in RWA behavior early in pregnancy (Figure 5D, interaction genotype × early pregnancy, p=0.01, F(1, 18) = 7.559, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for significant effect of time: Prlrlox/lox, p<0.0001, t = 9.307, df = 28; Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre, p<0.0001, t = 5.419, df = 28), the effect of pregnancy on RWA in the first few days of pregnancy (days 1–3) was subtly reduced in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice compared with control mice (Figure 5D, interaction genotype × early pregnancy, p=0.01, F(1, 18) = 7.559, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for significant effect of genotype: early pregnancy, p=0.0049, t = 3.329, df = 28).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: Prolactin action on arcuate kisspeptin neurons may play a small contributing role in the initial reduction in RWA during pregnancy, but this is not the major factor in mediating this response.
source: Thus, these data suggest the possibility that prolactin action on arcuate kisspeptin neurons may play a small contributing role in the initial reduction in RWA during pregnancy, but this is not the major factor in mediating this response.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the subtle reduction in early pregnancy RWA suppression in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice.

claim: Later in pregnancy, Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice and controls did not differ in their RWA.
source: Later in pregnancy, Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice and controls did not differ in their RWA (Figure 5B, total RWA day 15: p = 0.8949, t = 0.1345, df = 14; cumulative RWA days 16–18: p=0.7656, t = 0.3041, df = 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: The medial POA is a key site mediating prolactin action on behavioral adaptations associated with pregnancy.
source: Our previous work has identified the medial POA as a key site mediating prolactin action on behavioral adaptations associated with pregnancy (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: The MPOA has been linked to the hormonal regulation of RWA during the estrous cycle.
source: This region has also been linked to the hormonal regulation of RWA during the estrous cycle (Grigsby et al., 2020; King, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grigsby et al., 2020 and King, 1979.

claim: The MPOA contains the largest concentration of Prlr-expressing neurons in the hypothalamus.
source: The MPOA contains the largest concentration of Prlr-expressing neurons in the hypothalamus (Brown et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2010.

claim: Over 50% of Prlr-expressing neurons in the MPOA are GABAergic.
source: and over 50% of these neurons are GABAergic (Brown et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: RWA is inherently rewarding for rodents.
source: Moreover, RWA is inherently rewarding for rodents (Novak et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Novak et al., 2012.

claim: There is a Prlr-sensitive projection from the MPOA to the VTA.
source: and we have previously identified a Prlr-sensitive projection from the MPOA to the VTA (Brown et al., 2017), potentially impacting on dopamine-mediate reward pathways
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Prolactin action on behavioral circuits originating in the MPOA may mediate the suppressive effect on RWA.
source: Hence, we hypothesized that prolactin action on these behavioral circuits originating in the MPOA may mediate the suppressive effect on RWA.
evidence: This claim is speculative and represents a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: AAV-cre injection into the MPOA of Prlrlox/lox mice resulted in Cre-mediated recombination expression of GFP and removed all functional prolactin responses from this region, as determined by prolactin-induced pSTAT5.
source: Similar to what we have reported previously, AAV-cre injection into the MPOA of Prlrlox/lox mice resulted in Cre-mediated recombination expression of GFP (Figure 6A) and removed all functional prolactin responses from this region, as determined by prolactin-induced pSTAT5 (Figure 6A; Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: AAV-cre-mediated deletion of Prlr in the MPOA led to the mothers abandoning their pups following birth.
source: Replicating work we have published previously, this manipulation also led to the mothers abandoning their pups following birth (Figure 6B, number of live pups on day 3 lactation: Student's t-test p<0.0001, t = 10, df = 15), confirming the critical role of Prlr in this area for normal maternal behavior in lactation (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and a citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Mice with a specific deletion of Prlr in the MPOA did not show the immediate change in RWA once pregnant.
source: Mice with a specific deletion of Prlr in the MPOA did not show the immediate change in RWA once pregnant (Figure 6C, interaction virus injection × day of pregnancy, p<0.0001, F(21, 303) = 3.451).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: Mice lacking Prlr in the MPOA did not demonstrate any reduction in RWA in the first 3 days of pregnancy a time when dramatic reductions are occurring in controls.
source: Strikingly, mice lacking Prlr in the MPOA did not demonstrate any reduction in RWA in the first 3 days of pregnancy a time when dramatic reductions are occurring in controls (Figure 6C, interaction virus injection × early pregnancy, p=0.0267, F(1, 29) = 5.447, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for effect of early pregnancy: control injection p=0.01, t = 3.035, df = 29; AAV-cre injection, p=0.9687, t = 0.2256, df = 29).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: As pregnancy progressed, RWA remained higher in mice with a specific deletion of Prlr in the MPOA compared to controls.
source: As pregnancy progressed, RWA remained higher in mice with a specific deletion of Prlr in the MPOA compared to controls (Figure 6F: day 15 pregnant RWA: Student's t-test p=0.0036, t = 3.442, df = 15; Figure 6G: days 16–18 pregnancy cumulative RWA: Mann–Whitney non-parametric test, p = 0.0079, U = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6F and 6G with statistical analysis.

claim: The MPOA is a key site for prolactin-induced suppression of RWA during early pregnancy and for the maintained prolactin-induced contribution to attenuation of RWA throughout pregnancy.
source: These data indicate that the MPOA is a key site for prolactin-induced suppression of RWA during early pregnancy and for the maintained prolactin-induced contribution to attenuation of RWA throughout pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that MPOA-specific Prlr deletion prevents RWA suppression.

claim: RWA was low throughout lactation, apart from a small rise towards the last few days before weaning.
source: As reported previously, RWA was low throughout lactation, apart from a small rise towards the last few days before weaning (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

evidence: This claim is based on inference about potential confounds in the measurement.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice had significantly higher RWA in early lactation compared to controls despite similar pup numbers.
source: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice had significantly higher RWA in early lactation compared to controls (Figure 7A and C, effect of genotype: p<0.0001, F(1, 22) = 29.08, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for difference between genotype: day 1, p=0.0025, t = 4.472, df = 11.51; day 2, p=0.0057, t = 4.223, df = 9.628; day 3, p=0.0258, t = 3.391, df = 8.506) despite similar pup numbers (Figure 7B, Mann–Whitney non-parametric test p=0.2078, U = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and 7C with statistical analysis.

claim: For most of lactation, there was no difference in RWA between the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre knockout animals and the controls.
source: For most of lactation, however, there was no difference in RWA between the knockout animals and the controls (Figure 7A, interaction time × genotype: p=0.0194, Sidak's multiple comparisons test for difference between genotype: day 1, p=0.0196, t = 3.434, df = 72; days 2–20, p>0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A with statistical analysis.

claim: Prolactin action is not necessary for the sustained suppression of RWA in lactation.
source: suggesting that prolactin action is not necessary for the sustained suppression of RWA in lactation
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that RWA was similar between genotypes for most of lactation.

claim: Three out of five Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice each showed extremely high RWA on 1 day in mid lactation (days 6, 8, and 11, respectively), indicating that without prolactin action in the brain breakthrough bouts of extensive RWA are possible.
source: Interestingly, three out of five Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice each showed extremely high RWA on 1 day in mid lactation (days 6, 8, and 11, respectively), indicating that without prolactin action in the brain breakthrough bouts of extensive RWA are possible.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and based on inference about the role of prolactin.

claim: There was no significant difference in early lactation RWA for Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls.
source: There was no significant difference in early lactation RWA for Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice and controls (Figure 7B, interaction genotype × time: p=0.4394, F(92, 23) = 0.8525; effect of genotype: p=0.2292, F(1, 15) = 1.571).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis.

claim: During lactation, mice spent an extensive amount of time nursing offspring and were in a negative state of energy balance, either of which may impact the change in activity.
source: During lactation, mice spent an extensive amount of time nursing offspring and were in a negative state of energy balance, either of which may impact this change in activity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about lactation and speculation about factors affecting activity.

claim: Complete deletion of Prlr from the MPOA leads to abandonment of pups and termination of lactation, making it impossible to assess the role of Prlr in this area in the suppression of RWA during lactation.
source: Since complete deletion of Prlr from the MPOA leads to abandonment of pups and termination of lactation, it was not possible to assess the role of Prlr in this area in the suppression of RWA during lactation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observation that MPOA Prlr deletion causes pup abandonment.

claim: The mating-induced release of prolactin, acting through Prlr in the brain, induces a marked reduction in RWA in mice very early in their pregnancy, and this suppressive effect continues throughout pregnancy and into the first few days of lactation.
source: In this study, we have shown that the mating-induced release of prolactin, acting through Prlr in the brain, induces a marked reduction in RWA in mice very early in their pregnancy, and this suppressive effect continues throughout pregnancy and into the first few days of lactation.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: This profound behavioral response is likely an important addition to a range of hormone-induced metabolic adaptations that have been characterized to facilitate a positive energy balance during pregnancy, including leptin resistance, increased appetite, and reduced energy expenditure.
source: It seems likely that this profound behavioral response is an important addition to a range of hormone-induced metabolic adaptations that have been characterized to facilitate a positive energy balance during pregnancy, including leptin resistance, increased appetite, and reduced energy expenditure (Ladyman et al., 2018a; Ladyman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by citations to Ladyman et al., 2018a and Ladyman et al., 2012.

claim: From an evolutionary perspective, these changes can be viewed as adaptive strategies, enabling pregnant females to build up energy reserves in preparation for the pronounced metabolic demands associated with fetal growth and the subsequent lactation.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, these can be viewed as adaptive strategies, enabling pregnant females to build up energy reserves in preparation for the pronounced metabolic demands associated with fetal growth and the subsequent lactation (Butte and King, 2005; Dunsworth et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by citations to Butte and King, 2005 and Dunsworth et al., 2012.

claim: In our modern obesogenic environment, such changes have become maladaptive, contributing to excessive weight gain during pregnancy with the associated increased risk in pregnancy complications.
source: In our modern obesogenic environment, however, such changes have become maladaptive, contributing to excessive weight gain during pregnancy with the associated increased risk in pregnancy complications (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

source: Increasing numbers of women are coming into pregnancy already overweight or obese, and over 50% of women now exceed the Institute of Medicine (IOM) guidelines for optimal weight gain during pregnancy (Chung et al., 2013; Goldstein et al., 2017; Voerman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2013; Goldstein et al., 2017; Voerman et al., 2019.

claim: Increasing energy expenditure through exercise during pregnancy has become highly advocated as a therapeutic intervention that produces healthier gestational weight gain.
source: As it is difficult to alter energy intake, increasing energy expenditure through exercise during pregnancy has become highly advocated as a therapeutic intervention that produces healthier gestational weight gain (Sanabria-Martinez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanabria-Martinez et al., 2015.

claim: Despite pregnant women being well-informed about the benefits and safety of exercise during pregnancy, 60–80% of pregnant women do not engage in physical activity as recommended.
source: However, despite pregnant women being well-informed about the benefits and safety of exercise during pregnancy (Harrison et al., 2018), 60–80% of pregnant women do not engage in physical activity as recommended (Amezcua-Prieto et al., 2013; Gaston and Vamos, 2013; Hesketh and Evenson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harrison et al., 2018; Amezcua-Prieto et al., 2013; Gaston and Vamos, 2013; Hesketh and Evenson, 2016.

claim: There is a disconnect between knowledge and action regarding exercise during pregnancy, posing the question of whether there is a biological basis for decreased physical exercise during pregnancy.
source: This suggests a disconnect between knowledge and action (Harrison et al., 2018), and poses the question of whether there is a biological basis for decreased physical exercise during pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2018.

claim: Women report fatigue, pregnancy symptoms, and lack of motivation all as barriers to exercise during pregnancy.
source: Indeed, women report fatigue, pregnancy symptoms, and lack of motivation all as barriers to exercise during pregnancy (Harrison et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2018.

claim: The study describes a previously unknown hormonal mechanism that may be contributing to the loss of motivation for exercise in pregnancy.
source: Here, we describe a previously unknown hormonal mechanism that may be contributing to the loss of motivation for exercise in pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Three distinct approaches to deleting Prlr in specific neuronal populations each effectively prevented the initial pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
source: Three distinct approaches to deleting Prlr in specific neuronal populations each effectively prevented the initial pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main experimental findings from the three knockout mouse models.

claim: A broad forebrain neuron-specific deletion of Prlr using the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mouse blocked the pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA, implicating a prolactin action in the brain.
source: Firstly, a broad forebrain neuron-specific deletion of Prlr using the Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mouse blocked the effect, implicating a prolactin action in the brain, but this model was complicated by hyperprolactinemia and abnormal estrous cycles.
